title: Reverse a linked list: iterative (prev/curr/next) and recursive.
shortTitle: Reverse a Linked List: Iterative (prev/curr/next) and Recursive
keyPoints: The iterative method flips each next pointer to the previous node using three references: prev, curr, and next.
Saving next before flipping is essential, because once curr.next is overwritten the rest of the list is unreachable.
The iterative method runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
The recursive method reverses from the tail: the key line head.next.next = head makes the successor point back.
The recursive method uses O(n) stack space and risks stack overflow on long lists.
The iterative version is preferred in production for its constant-space guarantee.

s1_definition.oneliner: Flip each next pointer to the previous node, tracking previous, current, and next so the remaining list is never lost.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Iterative reversal** – walk the list with three references (prev, curr, next), rewiring each node's link to point backward, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
- **Recursive reversal** – reverse from the tail: recurse on head.next, then set `head.next.next = head` and `head.next = null`, in O(n) time and O(n) stack space.
- **Save next** – always save `curr.next` before overwriting it; otherwise the rest of the list is lost.
- **New head** – after iterative reversal, `prev` is the new head; after recursive reversal, the base case returns the new head.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh stores a chain of transactions oldest-to-newest and wants to display newest-to-oldest. He walks the chain and flips each arrow to point back to the node he just came from, keeping a note of the previous, current, and next node so he never loses the rest of the chain.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Iterative reversal of 1 -> 2 -> 3:

Start:  prev=null  curr=1  next=?

Step 1: next=2,  1->null,  prev=1  curr=2
        null <- 1    2 -> 3

Step 2: next=3,  2->1,     prev=2  curr=3
        null <- 1 <- 2    3

Step 3: next=null, 3->2,   prev=3  curr=null
        null <- 1 <- 2 <- 3

Return prev = 3.  List: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│       Iterative Reversal Flow                 │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                              │
│   prev = null, curr = head                   │
│       │                                      │
│       ▼                                      │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────┐         │
│   │ While curr != null:            │         │
│   │   next = curr.next   (save)    │         │
│   │   curr.next = prev   (flip)    │         │
│   │   prev = curr        (advance) │         │
│   │   curr = next        (advance) │         │
│   └────────────────────────────────┘         │
│       │                                      │
│       ▼                                      │
│   return prev (new head)                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a singly linked list means making the last node the new head and flipping every next pointer backward. The iterative method walks the list with three references: prev, curr, and next. On each step, save the current node's next, flip the link to point at prev, then advance both pointers. When curr runs off the end, prev is the new head.

Saving next before flipping is the critical detail. The moment you overwrite curr.next, the forward link is gone. Without saving it first, the rest of the list becomes unreachable.

The recursive method is elegant: recurse to reverse everything after the head, then set the successor to point back and null the forward link. But it uses O(n) stack frames, so on long lists it risks a stack overflow. In production, use the iterative version.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in the statement service. Transactions were stored oldest first but the view showed newest first. The iterative reversal handled long production chains safely, and the recursive version was reserved for clarity in short test cases.

Remember one sentence: save the next pointer before you flip the link, and when curr becomes null, prev is your new head.
